intro: The scherzo shares its musical world with Mahler’s song about St Anthony preaching to the fish. Continuous running figures support changing tunes and colours, until a late orchestral outburst disrupts the circulation. The song’s story offers a clue, not a literal programme for every bar.
question: When does repeated motion stop sounding playful?

sections.label: Scherzo · returning circulation
sections.mNote: the opening motion returns after the expanded middle

cues.title: Drums set the interval
cues.text: Timpani open with a dominant–tonic gesture: G to C, establishing the movement’s tonal ground before the running figures begin. Mahler’s heading asks for “quietly flowing motion”, not an ever-faster rush.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 80, opening timpani and In ruhig fließender Bewegung heading. The note introduces the opening passage rather than identifying an attack at the file’s first sample.

cues.title: Motion above and below
cues.text: Follow the running figures in both the upper and lower registers. Their persistence gives the movement continuity while shorter woodwind phrases interrupt or comment on the flow.
cues.evidence: Full score opening pages and the Foundation’s account of a double ostinato in treble and bass. The report confirms sustained attack activity through the opening minute; instruments are identified from notation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A sermon for the fish
cues.text: The related Wunderhorn song tells of St Anthony finding his church empty and preaching to the fish instead. They listen with apparent pleasure, then go back to their old behaviour. The poem’s circular outcome gives repetition a pointed context.
cues.evidence: German text of Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt, reproduced by the Mahler Foundation: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/wunderhorn-12/des-knaben-wunderhorn-12-songs-lied-6-des-antonius-von-padua-fischpredigt/

cues.title: A contrast within the flow
cues.text: The middle region changes the melodic emphasis without discarding continuous motion. Listen for a more clearly shaped phrase emerging from the same circulating world, rather than expecting a wholly separate slow movement.
cues.evidence: The score’s first contrasting passage at rehearsal 32 retains running figures. The report’s 1:54 novelty peak and immediate fall in level support an approximate boundary; the machine’s F-major estimate is not treated as a definitive key label.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Short phrases change hands
cues.text: Woodwind exchanges give the scherzo’s material different accents and colours. Try recognising the shape of a short phrase as it passes between registers, even when the underlying string motion stays much the same.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 86–90 gives successive wind figures and persistent strings. Strong changes at 2:32 and 2:44 locate this varied region broadly; no particular exchange is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Song and symphony together
cues.text: Mahler completed the song’s voice-and-piano manuscript on 8 July 1893 and the scherzo draft on 16 July. The orchestral song followed on 1 August. These closely spaced dates show parallel work, not a much later symphonic transcription.

cues.title: The middle suddenly expands
cues.text: A stronger and brighter passage enlarges the middle section. Listen for how the running background and more emphatic foreground coexist: the continuous motion can carry a larger orchestral gesture without disappearing.
cues.evidence: At 4:00 relative level jumps from the preceding −17 dB region to −7.2 dB, with increased spectral brightness and novelty at 3:58. The score retains rapid figures through the corresponding expanded middle.

cues.title: Another crest opens the space
cues.text: After a substantial retreat, the middle makes another strong arrival. Compare the brief crest with the more sustained singing that follows it; arrival and continuation play different roles in the phrase.
cues.evidence: Level drops to approximately −31 dB at 4:35, rises to −6.5 dB at 4:45 and settles around −15 to −19 dB after 5:00. Novelty peaks at 4:44 and 5:00 mark the change.

cues.title: Trumpets can sing softly
cues.text: The expanded middle includes a long trumpet melody above harp and string motion. Listen for connected phrasing rather than a fanfare: the brass can provide the lyrical foreground while other instruments maintain the flowing surface.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 100 shows the first trumpet’s sustained melody, accompanying trumpets, harp figures and strings in the E-major region. The report’s extended E-centred middle after 4:45 corroborates the broad placement, not a precise entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Words withheld from the symphony
cues.text: The scherzo has no singer, although its material is bound to a song. Mahler reserves an actual sung Wunderhorn text for “Urlicht”, the next movement. Here the orchestra carries the rhythms and contrasts without stating the fish-sermon words.
cues.evidence: The score’s movement sequence and forces; song relationship documented at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/

cues.title: The opening motion comes back
cues.text: The expanded middle gives way to the scherzo’s familiar circulation. Listen for the short running cells before trying to identify a complete melody: the return is carried by rhythm and texture as much as by a tune.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 105, rehearsal 43, asks for a return to Tempo I and restores short running figures. The cluster of report boundaries from 6:28 to 6:50 supports the return region; the map uses 6:50 provisionally.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repetition with changed emphasis
cues.text: Compare the returning material with the beginning. Repeated figures need not sound identical when a different voice is prominent or an accent falls more heavily; listen for what changes while the motion remains recognisable.
cues.evidence: A score-based comparison of the scherzo’s return with its opening. The note does not claim an isolated detected instrument or accent at 7:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A familiar contrast returns
cues.text: A lighter passage briefly separates the return from the approaching climax. Keep the earlier contrasts in memory: the scherzo revisits its material before expanding it beyond the scale of the opening.
cues.evidence: The report marks novelty at 7:54 and a drop from −12.8 dB at 7:50 to −22.8 at 7:55. Similar pitch-class profiles occur near the earlier 1:55–2:25 contrast; the exact thematic correspondence remains passage-level.

cues.title: The circulation becomes a crisis
cues.text: The late orchestral climax gives the flowing movement a disruptive new weight. Listen for the contrast between rapid figures and broad, emphatic chords: the music no longer behaves like a merely self-renewing dance.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 115–118 expands the brass, winds, percussion and strings into the late crisis. The report’s strongest windows cluster at 8:40–9:05, with its maximum at 8:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the cry
cues.text: The climax subsides into sustained sounds and returning motion. Mahler described the outburst as a cry of despair; its consequences matter more than the label. Listen for how the familiar figures resume after that interruption.
cues.evidence: Full score p. 118, rehearsal 51, shows a large diminuendo and returning low-string figures. The Foundation discusses the “cry of despair”; novelty at 9:16 and the fall after 9:05 support the aftermath region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass keeps moving
cues.text: In the aftermath, sustained upper sounds coexist with active lower parts. Follow the bass motion beneath them: a quiet texture can retain the movement’s restlessness even when its surface seems less crowded.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 118–120 contrasts long wind and string notes with divided low-string figures. The note describes a representative closing passage, not an exactly aligned bass entry.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last turn inward
cues.text: The final stretch contracts after another small rise. Listen for the running material losing weight rather than finding a broad, affirmative conclusion; the symphony will change its means of expression in the next movement.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −12.7 dB at 10:30 to −27 dB at 10:40 after boundaries at 10:20 and 10:32. The score closes the scherzo before the alto solo of Urlicht.

cues.title: Leave room for the voice
cues.text: As the scherzo’s final sounds die away, keep its continuous motion in memory. “Urlicht” will answer with a single human voice and a much slower, more measured phrase, changing both the scale and the kind of address.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −23.6 dB at 11:15 to −60.2 at 11:25. The score supplies the contrast with the following alto-led movement; this cue does not time that separate file’s entry.

transitions.title: Continuous motion supports a new foreground
transitions.how: The scherzo’s first contrast thins the texture and redirects the melody while retaining running figures. Bassoons and cellos help carry the change into the middle, whose later expansion reaches brighter major-key regions and a broad trumpet song. Continuity of motion links these contrasts to the opening: the music changes direction without simply stopping and beginning again.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 86, rehearsal 32, gives the initial transition; pp. 93–100 shows the subsequent expansion. Novelty at 1:54 and a level drop at 1:55 support the first contrast approximately; later events are not assigned to that instant.

transitions.title: The broad song releases the running figures
transitions.how: The broad middle loses its sustained melodic foreground as Mahler asks for the original tempo to return. Short figures reappear in the divided strings beneath lingering brass and woodwind sounds, reconnecting the music with the opening’s circulating texture. The return therefore grows out of the middle’s release rather than requiring a completely silent break.
transitions.evidence: Full score p. 105, rehearsal 43, Zum Tempo I. zurückkehren, with running low strings and retained trumpet harmony. Report boundaries at 6:28–6:50 and a sharp level reduction at 6:50 anchor a provisional return region.

transitions.title: The familiar motion becomes an outburst
transitions.how: The returning scherzo grows into a massed orchestral crisis. Rapid upper figures are reinforced by increasingly emphatic brass and low-register support, while percussion adds weight. The late B♭-minor outburst breaks the earlier balance between a mobile accompaniment and short melodic comments; it is an enlargement and disruption of the movement’s existing material.
transitions.evidence: Full score pp. 115–118 and the Foundation’s account of the late B♭-minor cry. The report rises strongly through 8:35–8:55; its maximum occurs at 8:55, within the marked span rather than at the join itself.

transitions.title: A long release restores motion
transitions.how: The climactic chords diminish and lengthen while short low-string figures begin to circulate beneath them again. Stopped horns, restrained winds and string writing reduce the weight without immediately erasing the outburst’s harmonic residue. The closing passage recovers the scherzo’s movement, but its restored activity is not a new grand conclusion.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 118, rehearsal 51, shows the diminuendo, stopped horns and low-string return; p. 120 continues the thinning. Novelty at 9:16 and the reduction after 9:05 support a broad aftermath boundary.

source.locator: Movement III, pp. 80–127; especially opening, rehearsals 32, 43, 50–52 and p. 100. Entries give representative scoring over provisional passages, not an instantaneous full roster; the concert’s edition is unestablished.

timeline.note: The opening dominant–tonic timpani gesture; its exact first attack is not sample-aligned.

Representative opening texture: circulating strings, woodwind interjections including cor anglais, and light percussion including the score’s rute; entries within the passage are not individually aligned.
The first contrast highlights a low-register melodic line and retained movement; this groups the transition at rehearsal 32, including the cor anglais participation on the preceding page.
Broad trumpet song above harp and string activity, as on p. 100; passage placement is provisional.
The return restores short string figures under lingering brass and wind lines, represented by rehearsal 43.
The late crisis expands to the massed orchestra; individual percussion and harp entries occur within the passage, not simultaneously throughout it.
Long upper sounds diminish while low strings recover short running figures; the roster highlights the aftermath, not every final-bar release.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
